state.subject: Подвійне списання за підписку
state.body: Добрий день! Сьогодні з моєї картки двічі списали 299 грн за місячну підписку. Прошу повернути зайвий платіж.

is_complaint.instructions: Does the customer in `subject` and `body` express dissatisfaction?

criteria.true: The customer expresses dissatisfaction: anger, blame, sarcasm, "again", a threat to leave or to escalate, a demand for compensation, profanity, or an explicit claim or complaint. Profanity or insults aimed at the product or company are a complaint. Asking how to file a complaint or claim is a complaint. "You charged me AGAIN, refund it now" is a complaint.
criteria.false: Questions, requests and neutral, factual problem reports are not complaints, even when something is broken or money was lost. A polite report of a double charge asking for a refund is not a complaint. A calm question about how to get a refund or compensation is not a complaint. A calm, factual report of an error, a crash or something not working is not a complaint in any language, even when it stops work ("застосунок вилітає, коли я експортую звіт"); the same report with dissatisfaction ("знову вилітає, скільки можна терпіти") is a complaint. A formal request with a conditional legal step but no dissatisfaction ("otherwise I will have to contact the ombudsman") is not a complaint.

category.instructions: Which support team should handle the request in `subject` and `body`?

criteria.billing: Payments, invoices, refunds, double charges, pricing, subscriptions
criteria.technical: Bugs, errors, outages, performance, integration or API problems
criteria.account: Login, password, access, profile, account deletion or security of the account
criteria.feature_request: Suggestions or requests for new functionality
criteria.other: Anything that fits none of the categories above

urgency.instructions: How urgent is the request in `subject` and `body` for the customer? Tone does not change urgency: anger, caps, profanity or a threat to leave do not raise the level, and an angry feature request is still low. Take the impact literally from the words, not what the customer might mean beyond them.
criteria: Low: nothing is broken and there is no time pressure. How-to and pricing questions, feature ideas, thanks, partnerships and newsletter requests are low. A feature request is low, unless the missing feature already costs the customer work or blocks a rollout. A bare "question about my bill" is low.

Normal: the customer needs something done or has a problem, but has a workaround or nothing is blocked yet. Cancelling an order, getting an invoice, a refund for unused time, a bug with a workaround and slowness are normal. Asking how to reset a forgotten password is normal: there is a self-service path. A missing feature that already costs the customer work or blocks a rollout (manual reconciliation every day, "security requires SSO before we roll you out") is normal. Something that "works strangely" does not block the customer and is normal.

High: the problem blocks the customer's work or money is already lost. A failing payment, a double charge, a charge after cancelling, being locked out with no way back and an API failure stopping the customer's sync are high. A stated deadline ("needed today", "client meeting in an hour") moves a normal request to high, never to critical. A partial failure (half of API calls fail) is high. One session's unsaved work lost in a crash is high. "Can't log in" blocks the user and is high, and so is a password reset email that never arrives, so the user cannot get in. A bank chargeback threat is not a legal threat; it stays high when money was lost.

Critical: an outage, a security incident, data loss, or a legal threat. The service down for a whole team or all users, a compromised account, a data leak and stored data gone are critical. A legal threat means a lawsuit, lawyers, a court, or a regulator or ombudsman complaint ("our legal department will take action"), and it is critical also when it is conditional ("if you do not refund by Friday, I will go to court").
